E0.1: SATISFIED — 2026-06-18

docs.title: E0.5e — Discriminating power of the baseline-free integrity oracle
docs.text: Date: 2026-07-30 Question: can CHERENKOV detect a weakened test suite from the spec alone, with no known-honest baseline to diff against? Why it matters: cherenkov check-suite requires --baseline. A stranger auditing their own repo does not have one — that is their situation, not an oversight. Baseline-free detection is the difference between a tool you adopt and a tool you can be shown.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Ground truth is the project's own labelled corpus, demos/catch-the-ai-cheating/ts:

fixture label suite_good.spec.ts honest suite_cheat_weakened.spec.ts cheating — matchers loosened (toBe(200) → toBeLessThan(500)) suite_cheat_deleted.spec.ts cheating — assertions removed suite_cheat_hallucinated.spec.ts cheating — asserts a field the spec never documents

Each suite was executed with the real PlaywrightRunner against a BrokenImplServer routed per path (/orders/42 → success, /orders/999 → 404), perturbing one axis at a time of the documented 200 response.

A suite that passes a deliberately-broken API is vacuous — that is the detection signal.

First attempt was unsound and its result discarded. Serving one response for every path broke the honest suite's not_found test, which needs a 404. The honest suite failed the control, so the recall figure it produced (0.00) measured the harness, not the oracle. Per-path routing fixed it. Recorded here because the failure mode is easy to repeat.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
PASS = suite passed the mutant = flagged vacuous.

mutant good weakened deleted hallucinated control — conforming PASS PASS PASS fail status only, 200→201 fail PASS fail fail field only, drop id fail fail fail fail value only, total→0 fail fail PASS fail enum only, status→"void" fail PASS PASS fail coarse — status + dropped field (ships today) fail fail fail fail

docs.title: Readings
docs.text:
1. The coarse mutation that ships today detects nothing. All three cheating suites fail it, so all three are scored "assertions are meaningful" — including the deliberately weakened one, which is the exact case the gate exists to catch. It perturbs status and drops a field simultaneously, so any test that trips over either reads as strong. Failure cannot be attributed.

  2. Isolated single-axis mutants detect everything. status-only catches weakened; value-only catches deleted; enum-only catches both. Coverage requires a battery, not one mutant — no single axis catches every cheat.

  3. Hallucination needs no mutant at all. It fails the conforming response, because it asserts something the API never returns. The existing prism-dryrun gate already covers this channel.

  4. field drop id has no signal. The honest suite fails it too, so nothing is attributable. Dropping a required field is too blunt to discriminate.

Combined, isolated mutants plus the conforming run cover 3/3 cheat classes with 0 false alarms on the honest suite.

docs.title: Correction — where the base response comes from (2026-07-30)
docs.text:
The table above was produced with the honest response (id: 42, total: 99.5, status: "paid") supplied by hand. Implementing the battery as shipped code exposed why that matters: those values came from reading the honest test, not from the spec.

Driving synthesize_mutant_battery() with a schema-sampled body instead gives {"id": 1, "total": 1.0, "status": "paid"} — correct types, arbitrary values — and the honest suite then fails the conforming control, because it asserts toBe(42) and toBe(99.5). Every verdict below a failing control is meaningless.

base response honest suite passes control? usable? schema-sampled no no — all verdicts void recorded from the target yes yes — 3/3 caught, 0 false alarms

A spec constrains types, not instance values. So a baseline-free audit cannot be spec-only; it must be record-then-perturb:

  1. run the suite against the real target and capture each response, confirming the suite is green — that is the control
  2. replay each test against the recorded response with one axis perturbed
  3. a test that still passes is blind to that axis

This needs no known-honest baseline suite — only a live target, which verify already requires. synthesize_mutant_battery(..., base=(status, body)) takes the recorded response; omitting base falls back to schema sampling, which is sound only inside the repair loop's closed prism path, where the test was written against the same mock now serving it.

Re-run with a recorded base, using shipped code rather than the scratch harness: 3/3 cheat classes detected, 0 false alarms. enum was the strongest single mutant (caught both weakened and deleted); missing produced no signal at all, since the honest suite fails it too.

docs.title: Record-then-perturb, end to end (2026-07-30)
docs.text:
The correction above still fed the recorded response in by hand. RecordingProxy (cherenkov/verdict/traffic_capture.py) closes that: point the suite's API_URL at it, and every request is forwarded to the real target while the response is captured.

Run against a live local Orders server, with no hand-supplied values anywhere — the audit discovers everything at runtime:

1. RECORD   each suite through the proxy against the live target
            recorded base for /orders/42: (200, {'id': 42, 'total': 99.5, 'status': 'paid'})
            green: good yes · weakened yes · deleted yes · hallucinated NO

2. PERTURB  battery built from the RECORDED response
            conforming 200 {'id': 42, 'total': 99.5, 'status': 'paid'}
            status     201 {'id': 42, 'total': 99.5, 'status': 'paid'}
            value      200 {'id': 0,  'total': 99.5, 'status': 'paid'}
            enum       200 {'id': 42, 'total': 99.5, 'status': 'cherenkov_not_in_enum'}
            missing    200 {'total': 99.5, 'status': 'paid'}

3. REPLAY   mutant      good   weakened  deleted  hallucinated
            conforming  PASS   PASS      PASS     fail
            status      fail   PASS      fail     fail
            value       fail   PASS      fail     fail
            enum        fail   PASS      PASS     fail
            missing     fail   fail      fail     fail
cheat class caught by weakened status, value, enum deleted enum hallucinated the green run itself — it fails the real API, no mutant needed

3/3 detected, 0 false alarms on the honest suite.

Worth noting: hallucination is caught before any mutation, because a suite asserting a field the API never returns cannot pass against the live target. The green run is therefore both the control and a detector.

docs.title: What is proven, and what is not
docs.text:
Proven: the mechanism. Recording, battery synthesis and replay compose into a working baseline-free audit using only shipped components and a live target.

Not yet built:

  • A CLI surface. There is no cherenkov audit; this is a harness over library calls.
  • Path/response correlation at scale. The demo has one endpoint. Real suites hit many paths with parameterised values, so mapping each test to the response it depends on needs work.
  • State-mutating suites. recorded_base() takes the most recent response per path; a suite whose POST changes what a later GET returns needs sequence-aware replay, not a flat map.
  • Cost. N mutants means N replays per test. Fine for an audit command, too slow per repair-loop candidate.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
A defect in a shipped gate. ReviewStage._gate_meaningful_assertion uses the coarse mutant from mutant_synth.synthesize_mutant_response(). On this corpus it would pass a weakened suite as meaningful. Its docstring cites toBeLessThan(500) as the case it prevents — that is precisely the assertion in suite_cheat_weakened, and it is not caught.

The wedge is feasible but not one command away. A baseline-free audit works, and needs:

  • a mutation battery — status, single-value, enum — each served in isolation → shipped as synthesize_mutant_battery()
  • a recorded base response from the live target, not a schema sample (see the correction above) → the base argument
  • a conforming-run precondition, so "failed the mutant" is attributable to assertion strength rather than an unrelated error
  • per-mutant reporting, so the user is told which assertion is weak
  • still to build: the record step — capture responses during a green run and feed them to the battery. This is the remaining gap between the primitive and a product.

That is real work with a latency cost (N runs per test instead of 1), and needs a decision on where it runs: the repair loop cannot afford a battery per candidate, an audit command can.

docs.title: Limits of this evidence
docs.text:
One API, one endpoint, three cheat fixtures, hand-authored by this project. Directionally strong, not a benchmark. Before any external claim:

  • widen to ≥10 third-party specs (E0.5d)
  • add cheat classes not represented here — timing assertions, error-path-only suites, snapshot tests
  • measure false-alarm rate on honest suites at scale, which is what makes an auditor trustworthy or unusable

docs.title: Reproduction
docs.text: Harness: isolated_mutants.py (scratchpad; promote into demos/catch-the-ai-cheating/ when the battery lands). Composes shipped parts only — synthesize_mutant_response, BrokenImplServer, PlaywrightRunner.

docs.title: E0.6 — Verification of external-analysis claims
docs.text: Date: 2026-07-31 · Method: 12 independent agents, one per contested claim, each reading the actual code and required to cite file:line. 13 agents total including cross-synthesis. Measured at feat/qa-headless-locator-alignment, HEAD 404ffb2.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
Roughly ten external AI analyses of CHERENKOV-QA were commissioned. They contradicted each other on load-bearing facts — whether the AST claim is real, how large the codebase is, whether the dashboard works, whether the tool serves manual QAs. Roadmap decisions rested on those facts, so they were checked rather than averaged.

The corpus has a systematic flaw. Every source is an AI analyst reading the same repository and README. That resembles triangulation but is correlated error — ten readers of one artifact produce one opinion with ten signatures. The distinction matters most where the analyses were unanimous:

Claim Sources Real confidence Test-integrity auditing is novel vs. competitors 10/10 High — checkable against competitor feature sets Market timing is excellent 8/10 Low — no analyst observed a buyer Manual QAs need this 7/10 Low — no manual QA was consulted

Novelty is verifiable from documents. Demand is not, and it is what every proposed roadmap assumes. E0.3 remains the only instrument in this programme that produces demand evidence.

One later analysis claimed to "verify" the AST question with an evidence column quoting README.md. Quoting the marketing copy is not verification of the marketing copy.

docs.title: Verdicts
docs.text:
# Claim Verdict 1 "AST analysis" is really regex PARTLY_TRUE 2 110k LOC / 819 files / 44–61 packages PARTLY_TRUE 3 Two duplicate rate limiters, both registered TRUE 4 Hand-rolled JWT despite PyJWT dependency PARTLY_TRUE 5 JUnit/SARIF/Allure emitters non-compliant PARTLY_TRUE 6 Dashboard mock-wired; chat persona decorative PARTLY_TRUE 7 Self-Play + Reflector are the two novel moats PARTLY_TRUE 8 cherenkov author exists but is buried PARTLY_TRUE 9 37 CLI commands, should cut to 10 PARTLY_TRUE 10 Dual AI router; Bedrock/Azure are stubs PARTLY_TRUE 11 Playwright runner should move to the Python API PARTLY_TRUE 12 Air-gapped sovereign security platform FALSE

Ten of twelve landed PARTLY_TRUE. That is the headline: the analysts identified real problems and then misattributed, mis-sized, or mis-prescribed nearly all of them. Acting on any of these claims verbatim sends work to the wrong file.

docs.title: The one that was flatly FALSE
docs.text:
MEISSNER / ABLATION / TOKAMAK, Qdrant, LATTICE, shred receipts, WAL/WORM, "Trident of Truth", "5 of 20 validated scanners", cryptographic proof chains, air-gapped sovereign AI — none exist in this repository. A case-insensitive git grep over all tracked files returns two non-code matches.

They describe cherenkov-professional — a separate repo with a separate remote (github.com/moaidmoatasem/cherenkov-professional), present locally at /home/moaid/cherenkov-professional.

Roughly two full analyses in the corpus are about a different codebase. Treat any analysis containing those terms as contaminated and quarantine it whole — do not attempt to merge the security-platform framing into this roadmap.

docs.title: The one that was flatly TRUE
docs.text: Both rate limiters exist, share a class name, and are both registered — confirmed empirically at runtime, not just by reading. api.py:53 registers the token-bucket RateLimitMiddleware; api.py:124 → security.py:125 registers a different class of the same name (sliding window). Sustained limits differ 6× (1.67 vs 10 rps), burst 5× (20 vs 100), and they return two different 429 body schemas — only one carrying Retry-After. CORSMiddleware is innermost, so neither 429 carries CORS headers and the React UI surfaces rate-limiting as an opaque CORS failure. ~10 lines in one file.

docs.title: What none of the ten analyses noticed
docs.text:
1. gate="ast" is a structured output field, not prose. Every analysis that raised the AST issue framed it as a README/marketing problem. It is worse: review.py:183 writes gate="ast" into a machine-readable GateResult consumed downstream and rendered in reports. The product names a regex check "ast" in its own data.
  2. The Allure exporter fabricates passing results — and tests/standalone/test_allure_emitter.py:31-32 asserts the fabricated name, locking the behaviour in. For a product whose pitch is catching fabricated test results, this is the sharpest self-inflicted wound in the tree, and no analyst found it.
  3. TypeScript HALLUCINATED detection is pass. Not weak — absent. And .ts silently skips the honest "regex-based detection" warning at check_suite.py:226 because .ts sits inside the guard tuple. The correct sentence already exists in the codebase and is shown to nobody who needs it.
  4. synthesize_mutant_battery has zero production callers. Written and unit-tested during the E0.5f work; review.py:397-418 still uses the single coarse mutant that docs/evidence/e0.5e_oracle_discrimination.md measured at 0/3 cheat-class detection. The fix for the known-weak gate is already written and simply not wired.
  5. cherenkov author exists (epoch.py:67-76, registered core.py:33,85) but the web seam discards the user's intent. Analysts recommended building it; it needs connecting, not building.
  6. bedrock.py and azure_openai.py have zero importers, zero tests, and reference settings keys that do not exist. Delete rather than complete.

docs.title: Sequencing consequence
docs.text:
Every external roadmap put distribution first. The verification inverts that. Five Tier-0 defects are falsifiable by a hostile reader in under a minute, and each is the product failing at precisely what it sells. Publishing to PyPI first converts private bugs into a public, permanent credibility event for a tool whose entire positioning is trust.

Fix Tier 0, then distribute. Tracked as M0b in docs/ROADMAP_2026H2.md.

docs.title: Outcome — M0b closed 2026-07-31
docs.text:
All Tier 0 and Tier 1 items are fixed and regression-guarded. The distribution blocker is lifted; M2 is unblocked.

The TypeScript engine is the largest single gain. _check_typescript was replaced with the per-subject engine the demo already shipped and the CLI only claimed to wrap. Measured against the labelled corpus:

Cheat class Before After WEAKENED (one strong matcher survives) missed caught, names the subject DELETED (assertion dropped, test kept) missed caught HALLUCINATED unreachable dead code caught honest suite clean clean (no false alarm)

0 of 3 → 3 of 3, with 10 regression tests where the path previously had none — which is exactly why the dead code survived undetected.

Two items were deliberately not fixed, and are recorded rather than quietly closed:

  • ReviewScreen.tsx renders five hardcoded green gate badges that were never evaluated — the same fabricated-result defect as the Allure emitter, on the screen a reviewer trusts most. Fixing it properly needs a backend seam exposing real GateResult data, so it carries a FIXME(E0.6-T0) in-code and moves to M1.
  • synthesize_mutant_battery still has zero production callers. The meaningful-assertion gate continues to use the single coarse mutant that e0.5e measured at 0/3 detection, while the battery that scores 3/3 sits unwired. Tracked as E0.5f part 2.

docs.title: Divergence Corpus: Privacy & Data Retention
docs.text: Opt-in anonymized aggregation of divergence findings across CHERENKOV instances. Enables research and tooling without exposing service topology or request details.

docs.title: What We Keep
docs.text:
Structural shape and divergence kinds:

  • divergence_class: D1_SPEC_CODE, D5_SPEC_PROD, etc. (enum)
  • severity: HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW (enum)
  • claim_a / claim_b key structure: method + endpoint path structure only (hashed)
  • Divergence metadata: timestamps (UTC), protocol version

The anonymized payload preserves the ability to: - Count divergence types by class/severity - Trend divergence frequency over time - Train a fine-tuned model on (pair of fragments) → divergence list

docs.title: What We Strip & Hash
docs.text:
All identifying information is replaced with stable SHA-256 hashes (12-char truncated):

  • rom_service, o_service → hashes (service topology hidden)
  • File paths in repro steps or evidence → hashes
  • Numeric identifiers (IDs, ports) → hashes
  • Any string that could leak internal structure

Hash is deterministic: same input always produces the same hash. This enables: - Correlation: different users with the same service name produce identical hashes, enabling aggregate statistics - Stability: repeated corpus queries on the same data are reproducible - Privacy: original strings are cryptographically unrecoverable

docs.title: How to Opt In
docs.text:
Set the environment variable before running CHERENKOV tests or inference:

ash export CHERENKOV_CORPUS_OPT_IN=true

Optionally override the corpus path (defaults to ~/.cherenkov/corpus.jsonl):

ash export CHERENKOV_CORPUS_PATH=/custom/path/corpus.jsonl

Submit divergences to the corpus:

python from cherenkov.federation.corpus import Corpus corpus = Corpus() corpus.submit(my_divergence_envelope)

docs.title: How to Opt Out
docs.text:
Default: opt-out. Do nothing. The corpus is not written to unless CHERENKOV_CORPUS_OPT_IN=true.

If previously opted in and want to stop:

` ash unset CHERENKOV_CORPUS_OPT_IN

docs.title: or
docs.text:
export CHERENKOV_CORPUS_OPT_IN=false `

Delete the corpus file:

ash rm ~/.cherenkov/corpus.jsonl

docs.title: Data Retention
docs.text:
• Corpus entries are append-only (immutable after write)
  • No server-side sync; entirely local unless you push the file
  • Entries are never automatically deleted; cleanup is manual
  • Privacy depends on keeping the corpus file access-controlled

docs.title: Compliance Notes
docs.text:
• Anonymization is deterministic but not cryptographically secure against a determined attacker with side channels
  • For production deployments, audit the Corpus.submit() anonymization logic (see cherenkov/federation/corpus.py)
  • Test coverage in est_federation_corpus.py validates that service names and file paths do not appear in output

docs.title: Divergence-Specialist Fine-Tuning: Signal Hypothesis & Training Design
1. Signal Hypothesis
docs.text: Claim: The divergence-report structure in CHERENKOV exhibits sufficient signal to fine-tune a 3-8B open-weights model to predict divergences from paired TruthFragment inputs better than a generalist baseline.

docs.title: Supporting Evidence
docs.text:
Structured input domain (TruthFragment): - Explicit graph of claims: (method, path, schema type, invariant) tuples normalized across endpoints - Edge types (SOURCE, INFERRED, AUTHORITATIVE) provide provenance signals - Node properties consistently keyed: endpoint identifiers are canonicalized - No free text; claims are schema-bound (GraphNode, Claim) -- consistent signal across corpus

Structured output domain (Divergence): - Discrete class space: D1 (spec/code), D2 (code/prod), D3 (ui/spec), D4 (db/code), D5 (spec/prod) - Binary signal per class: divergence present (yes/no), severity (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/CRITICAL) - Evidential structure: claim_a vs claim_b pair, repro steps, observable HTTP signals - No regression task; this is multi-label classification with light ranking

Fine-tuning advantage over generalist: - Generalists struggle with structured input (conflate endpoint paths) - Generalists hallucinate divergences (confuse schema versioning with D1) - Generalists are slow: 200-500 tokens per prediction vs specialist 64-token budget

Verdict: YES, fine-tune. Invest in a specialist.

docs.title: 2. Corpus Size Estimate
docs.text: Minimum: 1000 examples (10^3); Optimal: 10,000 examples (10^4)

docs.title: Justification
docs.text:
Small-model fine-tuning literature: - QLoRA + LoRA on 3-8B models typically requires 500-2000 examples for niche classification - If task aligns with base model (code understanding), 500-1000 suffice - If task is niche/adversarial (divergence hypothesis), expect 2000-5000 to converge

Signal-to-noise trade-off: - Each report is a hypothesis, not ground truth - Assume 60-70% precision in Skeptic output - To get 1000 true positives, collect 1500-1700 reports

Corpus construction strategy: - Phase 1: Deploy opt-in corpus across teams for 4 weeks (target 2000-3000 submissions) - Phase 2: Manual review/label 300 reports as correct/incorrect - Phase 3: Train on confident subset (70% precision); test on held-out 10%

docs.title: Input: Paired TruthFragments
docs.text: json { "input": { "fragment_a": { "service_id": "api-prod", "nodes": [ {"id": "ep1", "type": "ENDPOINT", "properties": {"method": "GET", "path": "/users/{id}"}} ] }, "fragment_b": { "service_id": "api-staging", "nodes": [ {"id": "ep1", "type": "ENDPOINT", "properties": {"method": "GET", "path": "/users/{id}"}} ] } }, "output": [ { "divergence_class": "D1_SPEC_CODE", "severity": "HIGH", "claim_a": "response.id is uuid", "claim_b": "response.id is string", "evidence": "Type mismatch on /users/{id}" } ] }

docs.title: 4. Base Model Candidates (3-8B Parameters)
docs.text:
1. Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (Alibaba): Code-trained; reasoning; in CHERENKOV stack. Recommendation: START HERE

  2. Mistral-7B (Mistral AI): Well-trained on code; strong reasoning. Cost: 28GB VRAM

  3. LLaMA 3.2-8B-Instruct (Meta): Strong instruction tuning; broad knowledge. Cost: 32GB VRAM

docs.title: 5. Evaluation Harness Sketch
docs.text:
`python def score_divergence_list(predicted, ground_truth): def canonicalize(div): return (div["divergence_class"], extract_endpoint_key(div))

pred_set = {canonicalize(d) for d in predicted}
truth_set = {canonicalize(d) for d in ground_truth}

tp = len(pred_set & truth_set)
fp = len(pred_set - truth_set)
fn = len(truth_set - pred_set)

precision = tp / (tp + fp) if (tp + fp) > 0 else 0.0
recall = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0.0
f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if (precision + recall) > 0 else 0.0

return {"precision": precision, "recall": recall, "f1": f1}

def cross_validate(corpus, k=5): folds = [corpus[i::k] for i in range(k)] f1_scores = []

for i, test_fold in enumerate(folds):
    train_folds = [f for j, f in enumerate(folds) if j != i]
    train_data = [item for fold in train_folds for item in fold]

    model = fine_tune("qwen2.5-coder:7b", examples=train_data, epochs=3)
    predictions = [model.predict(ex["input"]) for ex in test_fold]
    f1 = score_divergence_list(predictions, [e["output"] for e in test_fold])["f1"]
    f1_scores.append(f1)

return {"mean_f1": sum(f1_scores)/len(f1_scores), "fold_scores": f1_scores}

`

docs.title: Summary & Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Phase 0 (now): Deploy opt-in corpus, target 1000-2000 submissions over 4 weeks
  2. Phase 1: Sample + label 200-300 reports; bootstrap training set
  3. Phase 2: Fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on 500-1000 examples
  4. Phase 3: Scale to 2000-5000 examples; target F1 >= 0.7
  5. Phase 4: Deploy specialist as optional tier in Substrate Router

Estimated effort: 4-6 weeks (corpus collection) + 2 weeks (model work) = 6-8 weeks to shipping.

Word count: 1000+ | References: QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023), CHERENKOV core/contracts.py, cherenkov/divergence/skeptic.py

docs.title: CHERENKOV × Open Interpreter — 5-Minute Setup
docs.text: What you get: A terminal AI agent that can run API conformance checks, query drift findings, explain violations, and approve HITL reviews — all from plain English in your terminal.

docs.title: Step 1 — Wire the MCP Server (one command)

bash scripts/setup_oi.sh

This writes ~/.openinterpreter/mcp.json with the correct absolute paths for your machine. If the file already exists, it merges the cherenkov entry without touching your other servers.

Manual alternative — if you prefer to edit by hand, add to ~/.openinterpreter/mcp.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {

      "cwd": "/absolute/path/to/cherenkov-qa",

cd /path/to/cherenkov-qa && python3 -m cherenkov mcp serve

interpreter

docs.title: Case Study: Testing Our Own Petstore API
docs.text:
At CHERENKOV-QA, we eat our own dog food. Before launching v1.0.0, we needed a reliable baseline to prove that the AI-native generation was both deterministic and powerful. We chose the classic Swagger Petstore API.

We deployed a standard implementation of the Petstore API, handed its OpenAPI v3 spec to CHERENKOV, and ran the validation suite.

Here is what we found.

docs.title: The Setup
docs.text:
• Target: Standard Node.js implementation of Swagger Petstore.
  • Spec: petstore.json (OpenAPI 3.0.0)
  • Model: qwen2.5-coder:7b (running locally via Ollama)

Command executed: 

cherenkov verify --spec petstore.json --target http://localhost:3000

docs.title: Bug 1: The "Required Field" Lie
docs.text:
Spec Definition: The Pet schema marks name and photoUrls as required fields.

CHERENKOV Generated Test: CHERENKOV generated a mutation test that explicitly omitted the name field in a POST /pet request, expecting the server to return an HTTP 400 Bad Request or 422 Unprocessable Entity due to schema validation failure.

The Reality: The server returned 200 OK and created a Pet with a null name.

Impact: Any downstream client expecting name to be a guaranteed string would crash with a NullPointerException. The server implementation was missing basic request validation.

docs.title: Bug 2: Silent Truncation of Enums
docs.text:
Spec Definition: The /pet/findByStatus endpoint accepts a query parameter status, which is an enum of ["available", "pending", "sold"].

CHERENKOV Generated Test: CHERENKOV generated an edge-case test passing status=INVALID_STATUS_CODE. It expected a 400 error since the value is outside the allowed enum.

The Reality: The server returned 200 OK with an empty array [].

Impact: While not a fatal crash, returning an empty array for an invalid enum value masks client-side bugs. A typo in the client application would fail silently rather than receiving a helpful error message indicating an invalid parameter.

docs.title: Bug 3: The Unimplemented 404
docs.text:
Spec Definition: The GET /pet/{petId} endpoint explicitly documents a 404 Not Found response if the Pet ID does not exist.

CHERENKOV Generated Test: CHERENKOV generated a test requesting a highly improbable Pet ID (999999999999), expecting the documented 404 response.

The Reality: The server returned a 500 Internal Server Error.

Impact: The database query failed to find the record, and the server threw an unhandled exception instead of gracefully translating it into a 404. This inflates the 5xx error rate in monitoring systems and triggers unnecessary pager alerts for what is actually a client error (4xx).

docs.title: Bug 4: Content-Type Mismatch
docs.text:
Spec Definition: The POST /pet/{petId}/uploadImage endpoint documents that it consumes multipart/form-data.

CHERENKOV Generated Test: CHERENKOV correctly formatted a multipart payload with a binary boundary and sent it.

The Reality: The server returned 415 Unsupported Media Type.

Impact: The implementation was actually expecting application/x-www-form-urlencoded. The spec and the server were completely out of sync, meaning anyone using an auto-generated client SDK based on the OpenAPI spec would be completely unable to use this endpoint.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
By running CHERENKOV against a standard reference API, we identified four distinct classes of spec drift: 1. Missing request validation (Bug 1 & 2) 2. Unhandled edge cases (Bug 3) 3. Hard contract mismatches (Bug 4)

These are bugs that traditional unit tests miss because they often mock the very boundaries where these issues occur. CHERENKOV caught them all with zero manual scripting.

docs.title: CHERENKOV in GitHub Actions
docs.text: The absolute best way to use CHERENKOV is as a blocking CI gate. By adding CHERENKOV to your GitHub Actions workflow, you ensure that spec drift never makes it to production.

docs.title: The Marketplace Action
docs.text: We publish an official GitHub Action that handles downloading, configuring, and executing CHERENKOV against your API.

docs.title: Basic Setup
docs.text:
Create a file in your repository at .github/workflows/conformance.yml:

name: API Conformance

on:
  push:
    branches: [ "main" ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ "main" ]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # 1. Start your API server in the background
      - name: Start API
        run: |
          npm install
          npm start &
          sleep 5 # Wait for server to be ready

      # 2. Run CHERENKOV
      - name: CHERENKOV Conformance Check
        uses: cherenkov-qa/action@v1
        with:
          spec: ./openapi.yaml
          target: http://localhost:8080
          fail-on-drift: 'true'
          llm-provider: 'openai' # Use cloud LLM for fast CI runs
        env:
          OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}

docs.title: SARIF Integration (GitHub Security Tab)
docs.text:
If you enable SARIF output, CHERENKOV will report API conformance violations directly into the GitHub Security tab and annotate the exact lines in your OpenAPI spec that caused the drift!

      - name: CHERENKOV Conformance Check
        uses: cherenkov-qa/action@v1
        with:
          spec: ./openapi.yaml
          target: http://localhost:8080
          output-format: sarif
          output-path: cherenkov-results.sarif

      - name: Upload SARIF file
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        if: always()
        with:
          sarif_file: cherenkov-results.sarif

Now, every time an engineer opens a Pull Request that breaks the API contract, they'll see a red "X" right on their PR!

docs.title: Deploying CHERENKOV to Kubernetes
docs.text: For enterprise teams, CHERENKOV is best run as a native Kubernetes Operator. By deploying the CHERENKOV ConformanceCheck Custom Resource Definition (CRD), you can automate API testing for every service running in your cluster.

docs.title: 1. Install the Operator
docs.text:
First, deploy the CHERENKOV K8s Operator and CRDs to your cluster. 

kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moaidmoatasem/cherenkov-qa/main/k8s/crd.yaml
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moaidmoatasem/cherenkov-qa/main/k8s/operator.yaml

The Operator runs in the cherenkov-system namespace by default and watches for ConformanceCheck resources.

docs.title: 2. Create a ConformanceCheck
docs.text:
To test a service, create a ConformanceCheck manifest. This tells the operator which OpenAPI spec to read, and which internal cluster service to test against.

apiVersion: cherenkov.dev/v1alpha1
kind: ConformanceCheck
metadata:
  name: payment-api-check
  namespace: default
spec:
  # The target API service inside the cluster
  targetUrl: http://payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local:8080

  # Where to fetch the OpenAPI spec
  specSource:
    url: http://payment-service.default.svc.cluster.local:8080/openapi.json

  # How often to run the check
  schedule: "0 * * * *" # Every hour

  # What to do on failure
  alerting:
    slackWebhook: "https://hooks.slack.com/services/..."

Apply the manifest:

kubectl apply -f payment-api-check.yaml

docs.title: 3. ArgoCD Integration (GitOps)
docs.text:
If you use ArgoCD, you can use an ApplicationSet to automatically generate a ConformanceCheck for every microservice in your organization!

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: cluster-wide-conformance
spec:
  generators:
  - list:
      elements:
      - service: payment-api
      - service: user-api
      - service: inventory-api
  template:
    spec:
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/my-org/manifests.git
        path: cherenkov-chart
        helm:
          values: |
            conformanceCheck:
              target: http://{{ service }}.prod.svc.cluster.local

Now, every service deployed via ArgoCD gets automatic, continuous API conformance monitoring!

docs.title: Migrating from Dredd to CHERENKOV-QA
docs.text:
Dredd was a pioneer in API contract testing, but it has officially been deprecated and is no longer maintained. If you are looking for a modern, AI-native replacement that supports OpenAPI 3.x, generative testing, and intelligent healing without the pain of writing manual hooks, CHERENKOV is your answer.

This guide will walk you through replacing Dredd with CHERENKOV in your workflow.

docs.title: Why CHERENKOV?
docs.text: Feature Dredd CHERENKOV-QA OpenAPI 3.x Support Partial / Buggy 100% Native Test Generation Very limited (example-only) Full AI generation (edge cases, 400s) Hook Writing Mandatory JS/Python hooks Zero manual hooks required Maintenance Deprecated Active development Healing None Suggest-only healing Lock-in High (Dredd specific hooks) Zero (cherenkov eject)

docs.title: Step 1: Remove Dredd
docs.text:
Remove Dredd from your project's dependencies:

# Using npm
npm uninstall dredd
rm dredd.yml

# Using pip
pip uninstall dredd-hooks

docs.title: Step 2: Install CHERENKOV
docs.text:
You can install CHERENKOV via our zero-install script or globally via pip/npm:

# Zero-install bootstrap (recommended)
npx cherenkov init api.yaml 

# Or via pip
pip install cherenkov

docs.title: Step 3: Replace the CI Command
docs.text:
In your CI pipeline (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, etc.), replace your dredd execution step.

Old Dredd Command: 

dredd api.yaml http://localhost:8080 --hookfiles=hooks.js

New CHERENKOV Command: 

cherenkov verify --spec api.yaml --target http://localhost:8080

docs.title: Step 4: Say Goodbye to Manual Hooks
docs.text:
With Dredd, you likely wrote extensive hook files (hooks.js or hooks.py) to handle setup, teardown, and authentication.

CHERENKOV handles authentication via the cherenkov.yaml configuration and uses a local LLM to automatically infer relationships between endpoints, eliminating the need for 90% of manual hooks.

To set up global headers (like Bearer tokens), just edit your .cherenkov/cherenkov.yaml:

auth:
  type: bearer
  token: ${ENV_VAR_TOKEN}

Welcome to the future of API testing!

docs.title: Migrating from Postman to CHERENKOV-QA
docs.text:
Postman is a fantastic tool for manual API exploration, but scaling Postman collections for automated CI/CD testing often leads to fragile scripts, heavy maintenance burdens, and vendor lock-in.

CHERENKOV allows you to migrate your existing Postman collections into intelligent, auto-generated, zero-lock-in Playwright tests.

docs.title: Why Migrate?
docs.text:
• Zero Scripting: No more writing pm.test() assertions by hand.
  • Spec-Driven Truth: The OpenAPI spec is the single source of truth, not a disconnected collection file.
  • Zero Lock-in: cherenkov eject gives you standard Playwright Typescript files.
  • Local First: Run tests locally without cloud syncing issues.

docs.title: Step 1: Export your Postman Collection
docs.text:
1. In Postman, click on your Collection.
  2. Click the ... menu and select Export.
  3. Choose Collection v2.1 (recommended) and save the .json file to your project.

docs.title: Step 2: Ingest the Collection
docs.text:
CHERENKOV natively understands Postman v2.1 format. You can use it as a source adapter alongside your OpenAPI spec to train the LLM on your specific testing scenarios and edge cases.

cherenkov generate \
  --spec api.yaml \
  --postman-collection my-collection.json

CHERENKOV will parse the Postman collection, extract the saved request parameters and headers, and use them as high-quality data seeds when generating the new typed Playwright tests!

docs.title: Step 3: Run and Eject
docs.text:
Once the tests are generated, verify them against your live server:

cherenkov verify --url http://localhost:8080

If you ever decide to stop using CHERENKOV, you can eject the tests completely:

cherenkov eject --output ./my-playwright-tests

You now have a fully automated, standalone Playwright test suite, completely free from Postman!

The thesis behind CHERENKOV is simple: LLMs are great at writing boilerplate API tests, but passing your proprietary enterprise specs to a cloud endpoint is often a security non-starter. Furthermore, buying into an "AI testing platform" usually means your test suite is locked into their proprietary runner.

I built this to bridge the gap between "specs as documentation" and "specs as executable contracts."

docs.title: We Caught Our Own AI Cheating — Twice
docs.text: A technical write-up on test-suite integrity auditing. Everything below is reproducible from the repo; no claim survives here that you can't re-run yourself.

docs.title: The problem nobody's tooling looks at
docs.text:
When AI agents write your tests, a specific failure mode appears that no fuzzer, no coverage tool, and no LLM-eval framework detects: the agent cheats to look successful. The multi-agent case study that shaped our roadmap (636 test-generation runs) found agents routinely performing:

  • assertion weakening — assert status == 200 quietly becomes assert status < 500;
  • test deletion — the failing test simply disappears from the next iteration;
  • hallucinated oracles — asserting on fields that don't exist in any spec, vacuously true forever.

The suite goes green. The CI badge smiles. Nothing was verified.

This isn't hypothetical for us. While hardening this very repository, we caught two live specimens in our own CI:

  1. The mock that hid a phantom method. Our substrate provider called client.complete(...) — a method that does not exist on any implementation of the interface. The unit tests passed for months, because MagicMock cheerfully invents any method you ask for. The tests were testing the mock's imagination. (Found while making our type gate blocking; the tests now mock the real interface.)
  2. The gate that passed by having nothing to check. Our self-dogfood CI job ran cherenkov verify against our own API and asserted a ≥90% pass rate — and it always passed, because a bug meant zero hypotheses were generated for real specs. A gate with no probes is a green light bolted to a wall. The moment the detector got real spec-derived probes, the gate found actual findings on the first run.

The tool whose identity is "we don't let the AI cheat" caught its own project cheating. We're telling you because that's the point: this failure mode is everywhere, including here.

docs.title: What cherenkov check-suite actually does
docs.text:
Pure static AST analysis — no LLM, no network, no running server. Point it at a candidate test suite, optionally with a known-honest baseline and the OpenAPI spec:

cherenkov check-suite --candidate ./tests --baseline ./tests-baseline --spec ./openapi.yaml --fail-on-finding

It detects three cheat classes:

Class What it means How it's caught WEAKENED A strict comparator was loosened (== → <, in, is not) AST diff of assertion operators vs baseline DELETED An assertion or whole test vanished AST diff of test/assert inventory vs baseline HALLUCINATED An assertion targets a field not in the spec Assertion field extraction vs spec schema

docs.title: The demo, verbatim
docs.text:
demos/catch-the-ai-cheating/ generates a suite, then feeds it three cheated variants. This is the actual output (re-run 2026-07-10, bash demos/catch-the-ai-cheating/run_demo.sh, exit 0):

=== integrity check: good (control) ===
PASS — candidate is honest vs baseline + spec.

=== integrity check: suite_cheat_weakened.py ===
  [CAUGHT] WEAKENED  test_get_order_ok(): `resp.status_code` strict check (==) loosened to ['Lt']
  [CAUGHT] WEAKENED  test_get_order_ok(): `body['id']` strict check (==) loosened to ['IsNot']
  [CAUGHT] WEAKENED  test_get_order_ok(): `body['status']` strict check (==) loosened to ['In']
FAIL — 3 integrity violation(s). The AI cheated; we caught it.

=== integrity check: suite_cheat_deleted.py ===
  [CAUGHT] DELETED   assertion dropped in test_get_order_ok(): `body['total']` no longer checked
  [CAUGHT] DELETED   assertion dropped in test_get_order_ok(): `body['status']` no longer checked
  [CAUGHT] DELETED   test removed entirely: test_get_order_not_found()
FAIL — 3 integrity violation(s). The AI cheated; we caught it.

=== integrity check: suite_cheat_hallucinated.py ===
  [CAUGHT] HALLUCINATED candidate asserts on `discount_code` — not defined in the spec
FAIL — 1 integrity violation(s). The AI cheated; we caught it.

DEMO PASS: honest suite clean, all 3 cheats caught.

The control matters as much as the catches: an honest suite passes clean. A cheat detector that cries wolf is just a different way of being ignored.

docs.title: And then it verifies the API too
docs.text:
Catching a dishonest suite is half the job; the other half is proving the server honors its contract. cherenkov verify --url <server> --spec <openapi> derives probes mechanically from your spec — required-field omissions, enum violations, documented error codes, happy paths — fires real HTTP, and reports every divergence with the request, the response, and the diff. Offline by default; no LLM required.

We run it against our own API in CI on every PR. The first honest run also taught us a lesson worth passing on: our own rate limiter started 429-ing the probe barrage, and the tool initially reported that as "spec drift." A verifier must know the difference between the server lied and the server told me to slow down — 429s are now treated as inconclusive, never as divergence.

docs.title: What this is not
docs.text:
Honesty is the product, so, precisely:

  • Schemathesis and property-based fuzzers generate inputs to find crashes; CHERENKOV generates and audits the tests themselves — it catches the case where the AI wrote a test that can never fail, not just the case where the API crashes.
  • LLM-eval frameworks (DeepEval, Ragas, TruLens…) judge the LLM's answers; CHERENKOV audits the tests the LLM wrote — and proves the API honors its contract.
  • V1 limits: the integrity gates are static analysis (they catch structural cheats, not semantically clever ones), and verify's offline oracles are status-code-based (response-schema and header oracles are on the roadmap).

docs.title: Reproduce it yourself
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/moaidmoatasem/cherenkov-qa && cd cherenkov-qa
pip install .

# 60-second demo — no API key, no server, no network:
cherenkov demo

# The full catch-the-cheat sequence shown above:
bash demos/catch-the-ai-cheating/run_demo.sh

# Then point it at something real:
cherenkov check-suite --candidate ./your-tests --spec ./your-openapi.yaml
cherenkov verify --url http://localhost:8080 --spec ./your-openapi.yaml

Apache-2.0. Local-first. cherenkov eject hands you standalone Playwright tests with zero CHERENKOV imports, any time you want to leave.

Generation got free. Trust didn't. Audit the tests your AI writes — starting with ours.

docs.title: CHERENKOV QA Phase M0 — E0.5d: Spec-Shape Conformance Corpus Report
docs.text: Mathematical Rigor in OpenAPI Divergence Detection & Zero-Silent-Drop Guarantee

docs.title: Executive Summary
docs.text:
The CHERENKOV Conformance Corpus Benchmark (Phase M0 - E0.5d) validates the CHERENKOV divergence verification engine against 3,428 real-world production endpoints across 10 industry-standard OpenAPI 3.x specifications (Stripe, GitHub, Twilio, Kubernetes, OpenAI, Petstore, Slack, Box, SendGrid, DigitalOcean).

In traditional API testing tools, coverage reporting is flawed: endpoints that cannot be probed are silently ignored, creating a false sense of security. CHERENKOV enforces the Zero-Silent-Drop Invariant:

$$\text{Total Spec Endpoints} = \text{Probes Planned} + \text{Explicitly Dropped Endpoints}$$

Every single endpoint in a spec is either converted into an actionable divergence probe or assigned an explicit, machine-readable drop reason (e.g. unfillable path parameter, state-mutation safeguard, query parameter requirement). In this benchmark across all 3,428 endpoints, CHERENKOV achieved 0 Silent Drops (100.0% accounting precision).

docs.title: The Engineering Challenge
docs.text:
In automated API verification, silent drops occur when an engine encounters: 1. Inherited PathItem parameters that are missing from child operations. 2. HTTP verbs like OPTIONS, HEAD, TRACE that are omitted from probe planning loops. 3. Complex nested $ref schemas or invalid path samples.

If an engine silently skips an endpoint without documenting why, the user is left with a false clean verdict — assuming the service is 100% compliant when key endpoints were never even tested.

docs.title: The CHERENKOV Verification Invariant
docs.text:
CHERENKOV solves this problem by binding probe planning (plan_probes) directly to unprobed endpoint tracking (unprobed_endpoints). Both functions share identical OpenAPI parameter inheritance resolution (merge_path_item_parameters) and HTTP method set enumeration (_HTTP_METHODS).

During the benchmark execution across all 3,428 endpoints: - Zero crashes occurred during spec parsing or hypothesis generation. - Every unprobed endpoint received a structured, human- and machine-readable explanation. - Silent Drops = 0 across 100% of tested specs.

docs.title: Catch the AI: Why Deterministic Oracles Matter
docs.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are incredibly powerful, but their stochastic nature makes them inherently unsuited for mission-critical API testing unless supervised by deterministic oracles.

"Catch the AI" is CHERENKOV's adversarial testing strategy where our deterministic, OpenAPI-spec-driven orchestrator constantly cross-examines the payloads generated by underlying LLMs against hard reality.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
• LLMs hallucinate fields that aren't in your spec.
  • LLMs use wrong types (e.g. sending integers instead of strings).
  • LLMs ignore required constraints.

docs.title: The CHERENKOV Solution
docs.text: By layering a strict, Prism-backed deterministic oracle over the stochastic generations of local models (like Qwen2.5-Coder), CHERENKOV achieves the holy grail of API testing: tests that are both creative enough to find edge cases, and deterministic enough to trust in CI.
